query: For eutectic high-entropy alloys intended for structural applications, what single intervention could simultaneously increase strength and ductility? Formulate one testable hypothesis specifying the intervention, its proposed mechanism, the expected improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, the conditions under which it should hold, prior evidence supporting it, and an experiment that could falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a single processing intervention—cryogenic rolling followed by low‐temperature annealing—to an as‐cast eutectic high-entropy alloy (such as AlCoCrFeNi2.1) will refine its dual-phase lamellar microstructure and induce nano-twinning, resulting in simultaneous improvements in strength and ductility.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast eutectic high-entropy alloy with coarse dual-phase (FCC and BCC/intermetallic) lamellar microstructure.
generation.intervention: Subject the alloy to cryogenic rolling (deformation at cryogenic temperatures) followed by a controlled, low-temperature annealing treatment.
generation.conditions: The processing should be performed under conditions where cryogenic temperatures (e.g., near liquid nitrogen temperature) can substantially increase dislocation density and twin formation, and the annealing temperature should be low enough to avoid excessive coarsening, with subsequent mechanical testing conducted under quasi-static loading at room temperature.
generation.structural_mediator: An ultrafine-grained duplex microstructure featuring refined lamellar spacing and an increased density of nano-twins within the FCC phase.
generation.mechanism: Cryogenic rolling is expected to impose a high density of dislocations and activate deformation twinning, while the subsequent annealing stabilizes these microstructural features by relieving residual stresses without significant grain coarsening. This hierarchical structural refinement enhances work hardening and delays the onset of necking, simultaneously improving strength and ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the as-cast baseline, the processed alloy should display a marked increase in yield strength (potentially toward or exceeding ~1.2 GPa) while maintaining or improving ductility (elongation) by promoting enhanced work-hardening behavior.
generation.baseline: As-cast eutectic high-entropy alloy with a comparatively coarse lamellar microstructure and lower dislocation/twin density.
generation.boundary: The positive effects are expected as long as the annealing parameters avoid over-relaxation of dislocation structures; if the processing parameters (deformation degree, cryogenic temperature, or annealing temperature/time) deviate significantly, the beneficial microstructural refinement may not occur. Moreover, the benefit may be specific to EHEAs with an inherent eutectic lamellar architecture.
generation.uncertainty: While there is supporting evidence from similar thermo-mechanical processes in EHEAs, the exact magnitude of strength and ductility improvement, and their dependence on processing details, remains uncertain and requires experimental validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples of an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA: one set in the as-cast state (control) and one set subjected to cryogenic rolling followed by low-temperature annealing. Characterize the microstructure (using, e.g., SEM/TEM to observe lamellar spacing and nano-twin density) and perform standardized tensile tests at room temperature.
measurements: Microstructural analysis (grain size, lamellar spacing, twin density)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the processed samples do not exhibit a statistically significant simultaneous increase in both yield strength and ductility relative to the as-cast control, and if no clear refinement of the lamellar structure or enhancement in nano-twin density is observed, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Realizing improved strength–ductility synergy in eutectic alloys acting as in situ composite materials remains a challenge in conventional eutectic systems, which is why eutectic high-entropy alloys (EHEAs), a newly-emerging multi-principal-element eutectic category, may offer wider in situ composite possibilities. Here, we use an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA to engineer an ultrafine-grained duplex microstructure that deliberately inherits its composite lamellar nature by tailored thermo-mechanical processing to achieve property combinations which are not accessible to previously-reported reinforcement methodologies. The as-prepared samples exhibit hierarchically-structural heterogeneity due to phase decomposition, and the improved mechanical response during deformation is attributed to both a two-hierarchical constraint effect and a self-generated microcrack-arresting mechanism. This work provides a pathway for strengthening eutectic alloys and widens the design toolbox for high-performance materials based upon EHEAs. To tackle the aforementioned problems, eutectic HEAs (EHEAs) [] were proposed. On the one hand, EHEAs should have the general character of traditional eutectic alloys. In this sense, EHEAs should have better fluidity and thus better castability and less casting defects [,]. On the other hand, EHEAs as one kind of in-situ composites with lamellar or rod-like eutectic microstructures might reach the balance between strength and ductility via mixing the soft FCC phase with the hard BCC phase or intermetallic compound [,,,,,,,,]. Some EHEAs indeed have outstanding properties. Lu et al. [] reported the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA with simultaneous high strength (944 MPa) and good ductility (25.6%). The excellent mechanical properties do not depend significantly on derivation of eutectic compositions []. After cold-rolling and annealing, its strength reached up to 1.2 GPa and its elongation could remain at about 12% []. After cryo-rolling and annealing, its strength could reach up to 1.47 GPa while its ductility could even increase to 14% []. He et al. [,] designed the CoCrFeNiNbx EHEAs and found that the microstructures were stable from 600 °C to 900 °C.
